title: THE GUEST WHOSE HELLO WAS OUR GOODBYE
deck: Beings whose time runs against ours greet a Norrow graveside with what looks like a farewell, and anyone who reaches for them is hurt before they move. A child's funeral is set for dawn, and Illuminara has one night to find out what the visitors are doing, and to help a grieving mother meet them without deciding anything for either side.
shape: Seven scenes across one night to dawn: an order to seal; a welcome that looks like a goodbye; a clinic log in which injuries precede their causes; a kitchen where a mother chooses; two failed tests and a stone; a rite whose result is predicted before it is tried; and a lamp rule that outlasts the night.

scenes.title: The Order to Seal
paragraphs: *Sundby Head, above the town of Norrow · The evening before the funeral, 19:10*

By dusk the headland had been closed to the town for seven hours, and the few people who went up the cliff road anyway went in twos, with their lamps hooded, as though the dark were something that could be woken.

Illuminara came up the road with nothing but a coat and found the churchyard gate held by a young deputy whose left sleeve had been cut away. The dressing on his forearm was the colour of weak tea. Beyond him thirty headstones leaned toward the sea, and at the far end, where the grass gave way to rock, there was a place where the air was wrong. It had the wrongness of a held note just before it breaks. The grass blades there all lay pointing at the cliff edge, as if listening.

**Ivo Pell**  
Regional order, ma'am. Nobody past the gate.

**Illuminara**  
I'm not going past it. I'd like to talk to whoever signed it.

She did not have to wait. A woman in a grey regional coat was already coming up between the headstones with a clipboard under her arm and the walk of someone who has not sat down since morning. She had a face that had decided some time ago to be useful rather than liked.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Officer Achterberg. You're the one the mayor's office wrote to. I'll save you the trip: I'm sealing the headland at midnight. Iron stakes along the wall, a pulse charge on each, and the thin place closes the way the old one at Kell closed. I have six people in the clinic from the last visit. I don't need to understand these visitors to know they frighten my town.

**Illuminara**  
You're right that they've hurt people. I'm not here to tell you that was nothing. May I ask about the funeral?

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Linnea Voss, seven years old, buried at first light beside her great-grandmother, because her mother says she liked to be the first to see the water. I offered the family the lower cemetery. Mrs. Voss said no, and I will not drag a mother off a grave. So I seal at midnight, the funeral happens behind a closed wall, nobody in this town is hurt, and I carry that.

**Illuminara**  
And the visitors?

**Naomi Achterberg**  
They come at dusk and at dawn, and lately at the thin place's own hours too. They'll find a closed place. That's the point of a seal.

**Illuminara**  
Then one question before I tell you whether you're wrong. When did your six get hurt?

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Last Thursday. The funeral of the Brandvold boy.

**Illuminara**  
By the clinic's clock, I mean. Not by what anyone remembers.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
It's a clinic log, not a mystery. Read it. After that you go home, or I put you outside the wall myself.

**Illuminara**  
After that I'll tell you what I think, and you can put me wherever you like.

scenes.title: A Welcome at the Fence
paragraphs: *The churchyard wall, Sundby Head · 20:40*

They came without any sound. Illuminara, standing beside Achterberg at the low wall with her hands in her coat, felt the evening tilt, as a room tilts when someone leaves a door open somewhere else in the house, and the wrong place at the end of the grass began to glow the colour of wet slate.

There were three of them, tall and narrow and unhurried, grey as stone after rain, with faces turned a little aside as if they were attending to someone just out of sight. Each carried a length of cord that burned without smoke. A fourth walked half a pace behind the first. It was smaller than the others, and it held its cord low, as if it had not quite been given the right to raise it.

The first came forward to the iron fence at the head of the graveyard, thirty paces from the gate. There it lowered its cord to the ground, spread its open hands and bowed, slowly, with great courtesy. Then it turned and went back toward the thin place with the others, and a falling phrase went with them, four low notes, each a little lower than the last.
It was the most beautiful goodbye she had ever seen.

It was also what Marta Voss had come up the cliff road to see. She was a tall woman in a seamstress's black apron under a borrowed coat, and she had slipped past the deputy at the gate while his eyes were on the thin place. She was already halfway down the row of stones with her hand out.

**Marta Voss**  
Wait. Please wait. She isn't here yet, she's coming, they haven't even brought her. Wait!

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Mrs. Voss, back! Back from the fence!
Marta did not hear her. She reached across the last pale yard of grass toward the nearest of the departing figures, and Illuminara moved.

She crossed the grass the ordinary way, fast, took Marta by both shoulders from behind and pulled her away from the fence with all the gentleness she had, which was not as much as the moment needed. A ring of white frost bloomed round Marta's wrist. Her fingers had not reached the iron.

**Marta Voss**  
It's cold.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. Don't move your hand. Naomi, a blanket, now.

By the time the blanket came the figures were gone and the frost was melting, and under it the skin had gone the raw red of a burn some seconds old. Marta sat on the wall with her arm in wool, dry-eyed, like someone who had been ready for one grief and been handed another.

**Marta Voss**  
They were going away. They put the light down and bowed and left. I thought, they can't go, they haven't even seen her.

**Illuminara**  
Mrs. Voss, when you called out, were they already turning away, or had the first one turned its head toward you?
Marta shut her eyes. Beside her, Achterberg was very still.

**Marta Voss**  
It was looking at me. Before I called. I felt it look, and then I heard myself call, as if I'd heard my own voice already in my ear. I thought I was losing my mind.

**Illuminara**  
You weren't. The same thing put that mark on your wrist before you touched anything.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
You said that as if you'd known.

**Illuminara**  
I suspected it. Now I have it from your arm. I'd like to check it against the clinic's clock.

scenes.title: What the Log Knew
paragraphs: *The Norrow clinic, second floor · 22:05*
Edda Lindqvist, the night nurse, was a small, brisk woman who had logged six injuries in four days and disliked every time she had written. She put the ledger on the desk without being asked.

**Edda Lindqvist**  
Thursday's four came in together. I wrote what they told me, then what the monitor said, because I kept getting it wrong. Kjell Brandvold, frost-burn to the palm, 04:52. He says he put his hand out to the visitor at 04:57. I told him that couldn't be right. He said he knew.

**Illuminara**  
Hurt five minutes before he reached. And the ones who stood closest were hurt earliest. Whatever is near them isn't running the way we expect: the effect arrives, and a moment later its cause does. Call that the lead. It shrinks with distance, and tonight Mrs. Voss, at thirty paces, got seconds.
Achterberg did not say that it was impossible. She had stopped saying that around the second row of numbers.

**Illuminara**  
Do you have Thursday's recording? The deputy cameras.

The clinic's small screen showed a grey dawn, mourners in dark coats, a coffin carried on four shoulders to a grave beside a drystone wall, and then the slate-coloured light and the tall figures coming out of it. The leading visitor came to the fence, lowered its cord, opened its hands and bowed. It turned and went away. The four low notes fell behind it.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
You've shown me this. It leaves.

**Illuminara**  
Watch it the other way.

She ran the recording backward. The mourners unwalked. The coffin rose out of the grave into the hands of the four who had set it down, and out of the thin place the leading visitor came forward, unhurried, its cord raised in both hands. At the fence it lifted its head out of the bow and opened its hands palms upward at the crowd. Its phrase rose in four notes, each a little higher than the last.

**Edda Lindqvist**  
Like someone coming to a door.

**Illuminara**  
Look at what they're walking toward. A box coming up out of the earth into the arms of a family. For them it runs this way. They aren't leaving a grave, they're meeting one, the way you'd meet someone who is being carried in.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Or meeting something that's been dug up.

**Illuminara**  
It could be that. I don't know what they know. I know which way their hands are open.
Achterberg sat down on the edge of the desk, for the first time that day. She did not look relieved. She looked like a woman whose argument had been taken from her while the hazard stayed.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Say it's a welcome. Six of my people are in beds. Welcome or not, the bill is the same, and I can't make my deputies stand in front of something that wounds people before they're touched.

**Illuminara**  
I won't argue that away. The hazard and the welcome have one cause: whatever is nearest to them is answered before it asks. So no answer of ours can come first, and I'd like the night to find out what can. May I have until dawn? Nobody inside the fence line but people who have said yes, a deputy who can stand back, and your seal kept ready, so you can close the place the moment I'm wrong.

**Edda Lindqvist**  
Naomi. Before you answer. Three of my six won't come back to the headland for anything, and the other three said they'd stand at the gate with a bell if it came to that. Kjell said one thing and said it twice: whatever they do up there, nobody reaches.
Achterberg looked at the clipboard in her hand.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
The seal waits until dawn, and not a minute past it. The charges stay in the stakes. If anything is marked beyond what's agreed, I fire them, and you don't stop me.

**Illuminara**  
If I'm about to stop you, I'll have been wrong first.

scenes.title: What They Think They Are Coming To
paragraphs: *The Voss house, Norrow · 23:20*

Marta's kitchen smelled of lemon soap and of the long wait before a funeral, which has a smell of its own. Her father sat at the table with his back to the window and a mug of tea he had not touched, an old man with a gravedigger's forearms and a face carved down to its hardest lines. He had dug the grave himself on Tuesday. He did not look up when Illuminara came in.

**Aksel Voss**  
If you've come to ask me to stand beside one of those things, you may as well go home.

**Illuminara**  
I haven't come to ask you for anything, Mr. Voss. I came to tell your daughter what I think I saw, and she may stop me wherever she likes.
Marta sat at the end of the table with her wrist in the dressing Edda had put on it. She nodded once.

**Illuminara**  
I think they are arriving, not leaving. What we see as a goodbye is the last part of a welcome. In the recording they carry a light toward the grave and open their hands to it. I think that to them a gathering at a grave is a gathering for someone who is about to arrive. I could be wrong about what they know of her.

**Marta Voss**  
You're telling me they believe my daughter is being born.

**Illuminara**  
I'm telling you what their gesture looks like it means to them. I'd rather you had it from me than found it out at the grave. You may think it's a cruelty. You can still bury her in the lower churchyard, and I'll walk you down there myself.

**Marta Voss**  
I don't want the lower churchyard.

**Aksel Voss**  
Marta.

**Marta Voss**  
I know, Papa. I know what they did on Thursday. I know what they did to my wrist. I don't want them near her. But I want her at the headland, where she wanted to be. If there's any way they can be there and she can have the sea, and nobody is marked and nobody is frightened, I won't be the one who says no because I was afraid to be wrong about them.
She turned her wrist over on the cloth.

**Marta Voss**  
What would I have to do?

**Illuminara**  
Nothing, if you don't want to. But I think I know what the rite has to be, and I can't build it without you. The middle of it is yours.

**Aksel Voss**  
I'll not be in it.

**Illuminara**  
No one asked you to be.
The old man stared at the window, where there was only the reflection of the lamp. After a time he stood, took his coat from the peg, and went out without saying where he was going.

scenes.title: Two Failures and a Stone
paragraphs: *The churchyard fence · Night, 00:50*
She tried the cheap test first, because a cheap test is allowed to fail.

Ivo Pell had volunteered, and Illuminara had said no twice and then yes, because he would be at the fence tomorrow anyway with a rifle he did not know how to put down. He stood at the iron rail with a hand bell, forty paces back from the glow.
The visitors came at one. The cord raised, the hands opened, the turn, the falling phrase, the going.

**Illuminara**  
Now, Ivo. Ring it once, when the first one lowers its cord. That's our call. I'll watch for the answer.

He rang the bell. Its note went out thin and clear over the graves. The leading visitor, whose cord was already on the ground, lifted its head and turned toward him, and Ivo cried out and dropped the bell. On the inside of his wrist, above the old dressing, a ring of frost had risen.

**Ivo Pell**  
I hadn't done it yet. It already knew.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. It answered what you were about to do. Our call isn't the start of an exchange. It's the end of their answer. Go and let Edda look at that arm.

The second idea was the one Marta had asked about without knowing it. At two, Illuminara stood alone at the fence and said the child's name toward the thin place, once, plainly: Linnea Voss. The visitors shuddered in their places like grass under wind. The nearest was the small one with the low cord, and it turned its head from her. It made a sound she had not heard from any of them, a low confused grinding that was neither a word nor a note, and went into the thin place faster than any of them had gone.
She stood with her hands at her sides. She had learned what she needed. She had also made something afraid in order to learn it, and she did not pretend otherwise.

**Illuminara**  
The name reached them backward, the end of the word before the beginning. Not refused. Noise. And I did it to them on purpose.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
You had a reason.

**Illuminara**  
I had a reason. There'll be no more tests on them, Naomi. Whatever we try now, we offer, and they choose.
She stood a while longer, turning the grinding sound over, and it began to mean something else.

**Illuminara**  
It didn't flinch at a stranger's name. Their time runs against ours, so for the small one tomorrow's grave is already behind it. It has stood at that stone before I ever spoke. I didn't tell it something new. I said aloud, from the wrong side, a thing it was already carrying.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Then you frightened a mourner.

**Illuminara**  
I frightened a mourner and called it a test. That's the cost, and it's mine. It also means I can't say it came back to the stone after running from me. For it, the stone came first.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Then you can't call, you can't answer, and you can't even say the name.

**Illuminara**  
Not in sequence. I've been asking how to answer them, and that's the wrong question. Every act we do has a before and an after, and they see our before as their after. So I need an act with the same shape either way you read it: a walk to the grave and the same walk back, a lamp raised and the same lamp lowered, a hand laid down and the same hand lifted. Each of us begins at our own beginning and meets the other in the middle.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
And the middle?

**Illuminara**  
That's the trouble. Whatever stands in the middle can't be spoken, and it can't be moving. It has to be something the sequence doesn't change.
The sea was a long dark noise below the cliff. Somewhere in the lower town a dog began and stopped.

It was Achterberg who saw him first. A figure was coming up the cliff road in the dark, bent a little under something wrapped in sacking, his lamp putting his face in shadow and his gravedigger's forearms in light. Aksel Voss did not come through the gate. He stopped on the road, outside the wall, and set the sacking down on the grass.

**Aksel Voss**  
I'm not going to stand with them. There's a stone. I cut it Monday, before any of this. If I couldn't do anything else for her I could do that. It was to go on the grave after the earth settled. I hadn't meant to bring it up tonight.

He unwrapped it. It was a slab of grey sea-granite about the height of a child, rough at the edges and polished on its face, and on the face, carved deep and square with a mason's care, a single name: Linnea. Under it, smaller, the dates.

**Aksel Voss**  
It doesn't say anything. It just has the name. It'll have the name in a hundred years, and it doesn't care which way anyone's clock runs.

**Illuminara**  
Mr. Voss, that is the one thing in all this that doesn't change under reversal. A name said aloud is gone as it's said, and they'd hear it unwound. A name cut in stone is the same from either side of time.

**Aksel Voss**  
I haven't agreed to anything.

**Illuminara**  
No. You've given us the stone. You don't have to give us anything else.
He looked at his granddaughter's name. He did not look at Illuminara.

**Aksel Voss**  
It goes at the head of the grave, tonight, and I'll set it myself. And then I'll be at the gate. Not in. At the gate.

**Illuminara**  
At the gate is plenty.

scenes.title: The Order of the Rite
paragraphs: *The grave beside the drystone wall · Dawn, 06:20*

By first light the rite was one sheet of Achterberg's paper in Marta's handwriting, argued over line by line in the lantern light. Illuminara's part was smaller. She would set the opening of the thin place narrow, so the lead stayed at seconds instead of minutes, and then she would not touch it again. She could not hold it past sunrise.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Before we begin. What do I see if you're right? Not what you hope. What.

**Illuminara**  
Edda calls the lead by the second, from the frost on Marta's wrist, the way she called the injuries. While one side is doing something the other hasn't yet, a lamp lifted, a cord lowered, a hand coming down, there will be a lead, small. Once Marta's hand is on the name, and the visitor's is on the stone, and nothing moves, there should be none. Nought. I won't change the hold from the first minute to the last, so if it reads nought, it isn't me.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
And if you're wrong?

**Illuminara**  
Then the lead is still there while both hands are still, the place is not safe, and you fire the charges.

**Edda Lindqvist**  
One mark at the end, when her hand lands. Would you expect that one?

**Illuminara**  
I would. A hand arriving is the last thing either side does that has a before and an after. Once, three seconds, and then it should draw back.

**Marta Voss**  
And if they don't do any of it?

**Illuminara**  
Then you've still buried your daughter beside the sea, and I was wrong about the rest. They can't be made to do any of it. Neither can you.

The deputies stood along the wall with their lamps, a long loose line of dark coats. At the gate, outside the iron, Aksel Voss sat on an upturned bucket with his arms folded. Ivo Pell, refused the fence, had put himself beside him with the bell. Edda Lindqvist stood at the gate post with the ledger open and her watch in her hand.

At six thirty-two the wrongness at the end of the grass shifted. They came as they always came, three of them, grey in the half-light, faces turned a little aside. The smaller one walked half a pace behind the first, its cord held low. Illuminara could not have said whether it was the one that had run from her at two, and she no longer thought the question had the shape she had given it.

**Marta Voss**  
Now?

**Illuminara**  
Whenever you're ready.

Marta raised the lamp. She did it slowly, with her good hand, to the height of her shoulder, and held it there. The leading visitor reached the fence. It lowered its cord to the grass, spread its hands and bowed. And Illuminara, with her palms flat against the air in front of her and every muscle taut, watched it and understood that what looked to her like the start of a greeting was, for them, the last motion of a long approach, and that she was seeing it from the wrong end.

Marta walked. The lamp was steady and her feet found the grass between the stones without hurry, past her great-grandmother's name, past a stranger's, to the head of a small mound of fresh earth with a grey sea-granite stone standing at its head. On the stone, in the first yellow slant of the sun, was the one word.

The three taller visitors went down on one knee in a single motion, as a congregation might. The smaller one came forward between them as far as the stone and stopped an arm's length from it. Illuminara felt the lead tighten to a hair, and left the hold exactly where it was.
Marta laid her hand on the name.

She stood with her palm on the cold granite and her eyes on the carved letters, and the smaller visitor, a body's length away, laid its own grey hand on the other edge of the stone. A hand's breadth of granite lay between them, and a little more of air. On Marta's wrist the frost rose, once, three seconds ahead of its cause, and drew back. It was the one mark Illuminara had said to expect.

Then the stillness began, the one part of the rite in which nothing was done. Marta's lips moved once. Illuminara could not hear what she said, and was not meant to. The small grey figure lowered its head until its brow nearly touched the stone and stayed there, and the four low notes, rising now, as they always had for the visitors themselves, went out over the churchyard.

At the gate Aksel Voss stood up from his bucket. He did not come in. He took off his cap, stained dark with soil, and held it against his chest. Beside him Ivo Pell stood very straight, a deputy at a funeral, and had the sense to do nothing else.

**Edda Lindqvist**  
Nought.

She said it low, to the ledger, as if it might break. Illuminara heard it all the same. She had not moved her hands. The hold was exactly as wide as it had been a minute ago, and the lead had gone, at the stone, to nothing at all, as she had told them it would if she was right.

Marta lifted her hand from the stone. The visitor lifted its own. She turned from the grave with the lamp at her shoulder and walked back along the row of names at the pace she had come. At the fence the three kneeling figures rose in the same motion, and the smaller went back among them.

**Marta Voss**  
Is that all of it?

**Illuminara**  
Lower the lamp.

She lowered the lamp. The visitors lowered their cords. Four heads bowed together, and for the first time Illuminara heard the falling phrase and the rising phrase together, from the same mouths, as one, and she thought: it is the same four notes. It always was.

The sun cleared the water at seven eleven. The slate-coloured light folded in on itself at the end of the grass, and where the thin place had been there was only a stone wall and a gull and a wind off the sea. Illuminara took her hands from the air and found they were shaking so badly she had to sit on the nearest stone.

scenes.title: The Lamp Rule
paragraphs: *The churchyard gate · 07:45*

Naomi Achterberg did not fire the charges. She stood at the gate with the box at her feet, a little apart from her deputies, and looked at the grave, where Marta Voss knelt beside the settled earth with her hand on the stone and the sun on her back.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Nobody was marked.

**Illuminara**  
Mrs. Voss, once, before the stone. Then nothing. I didn't change my hold. The lead went to nothing when her hand was on the name, and Edda's watch says so.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
So it wasn't you.

**Illuminara**  
It was me for the first seconds and not me for the last. I can't be here for every funeral. The stone can.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
The headland isn't safe, then. It's only safer than my seal would have made it.

**Illuminara**  
It stays dangerous. Anyone who reaches for one of them without warning is hurt before they reach.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
Three of my six won't be back on this headland if I put a gun to them. That's a cost I can't write away. But I'm not sealing it. Not on your word. On mine. I'll say what I saw: a woman buried her child where she chose, with the visitors present, and the only one marked was the one who had agreed to the risk.
She looked at the sheet of paper in Marta's handwriting.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
A lamp rule. The headland opens to them, and to us, only when a lamp is lit at the fence by the family. No lamp, my people seal it within the hour. With a lamp, the order of the rite holds, and the only hand that crosses the fence line is the one laid on the stone. Everyone else stands at the gate, with a bell, and Edda's watch. It doesn't depend on there being someone like you. It depends on a stone, a schedule, and a rule that anyone can break.

**Illuminara**  
Anyone can. That's why it holds.

**Naomi Achterberg**  
And the rule is mine. I'd like it written so. I'm not betting the town on your sentiment.
Achterberg picked up the charge box. She seemed about to say something else, and did not, and went down the lane toward the ambulance.
Marta came to the gate when the sun was well up, grey with tiredness. Her wrist had stopped hurting, she said. She did not know whether that was the rite or the morning.

**Marta Voss**  
I don't know if what I thought at the stone reached them. I don't know if the little one understood a word.

**Illuminara**  
Nor do I. It was yours to say. I didn't ask what it was.

**Marta Voss**  
No. You didn't.
She looked at the stone, a plain grey slab in the morning light, with a single name on it and a gull standing on top.

**Marta Voss**  
They think she's coming, and I know she's gone. I thought that would make it worse. It only makes it strange.

**Illuminara**  
Strange isn't wrong.

At the gate Aksel Voss had put his cap back on and stood with his hands in his pockets, looking at the grave across the wet grass. He did not come in, then or later. When his daughter reached him he put an arm round her shoulders, awkwardly, an old man who had been dry-eyed since Sunday, and they walked down the lane together without speaking.

There was a lamp at the fence when Illuminara left, set on the iron where Marta had lit it, burning pale in the sunlight. On the bottom rail, in Achterberg's cramped hand, someone had tied a card. It said that no one was to reach for what they could not yet see. Under it a younger hand, Ivo's, had added: and if you are unsure, ring the bell.

Behind her the air at the end of the churchyard had returned to its ordinary colour. It would not stay so. The thin place was still there, and still dangerous, and the schedule might fail. But on the head of the small grave a single grey pebble now rested, set exactly in the centre of the name, that had not been there when the sun came up. Nobody had seen it set. Nobody ever knew whether it had been placed by a visitor in the first minute of the rite or the last, and for beings whose first minute was the last of ours, perhaps it was not a question with a single answer.

critic_line: Visitors whose time runs backward greeted a Norrow graveside with what looked like a farewell and hurt anyone who reached for them; Illuminara read the greeting by reversing the clinic recording, owned a failed test that frightened a mourner, and let a grandfather's carved name-stone become the one act that reads the same in both directions, so a mother buried her child by the sea and the town kept a lamp rule instead of a seal.
